content:
An interesting paper with a somehow misleading title: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08144. Not sure if it has been posted somewhere but I can't find anyone mentioning it.

The paper basically mentions a well known problem: there's no good way to guarantee that a formalization faithfully represents the informal proof, especially when the formalization is done by a LLM agent. The informal proof may be wrong; or it may be correct but the formalized proof uses a fundamentally different method that only looks close to the informal proof.

Such a disagreement between the formal and informal proofs does not invalidate the theorem but is detrimental to human understanding because most people still tend to read the natural language proof to understand it and may be misled by an incorrect "verified" proof.

Perhaps I'm naive, but I think in practice this problem can be easily mitigated by translating each claim in the informal proof as a have command. Then automatic tools can be used to extract all the have commands to construct a proof sketch that resembles a natural language proof which can be read by a human mathematician to decide how it compares with the original informal proof: such tools already exist in the Mizar ecosystem and produce informal-looking articles like this.
